network.overall_strategy: This connected bipartite network contains 24 molecule nodes, 19 reaction nodes and exactly 10 distinct target-producing reaction sequences. The pathways are chemically differentiated variants of photoredox/Strecker synthesis and glycine hydroxymethylation, not ten independently demonstrated prebiotic mechanisms. Three photoredox systems provide glycolaldehyde; each can feed immediate Strecker chemistry or a chemically justified bisulfite-storage branch. Two experimentally observed photochemical routes instead produce serine aminonitrile without externally added ammonia. Two further routes supply glycine for formaldehyde hydroxymethylation; the photochemical glycine-precursor entry in P10 is explicitly a mechanistic extrapolation. Formaldehyde, HCN, ammonia and inorganic reagents are declared initial inventories, not assumed products of an unmodeled discharge reactor. Their availability and concentration remain geochemical boundary conditions; atmospheric production does not establish the required pond concentrations. All productive sequences remain in Surface environments. Hydrothermal exposure appears only as an optional destruction branch. Numerical conditions distinguish reported observations from proposed environmental or experimental operating windows. Modern photochemical yields refer to aminonitriles, not free serine. Conversion through amides and subsequent preservation are explicit, incompletely validated bottlenecks. Photoredox sulfate, phosphate and S8 outputs are formal terminal redox-bookkeeping assumptions rather than measured primary coproduct distributions. Acid-base pools are represented by the listed constitutional species; pH-dependent speciation must be calculated before kinetic modeling. Terminal coproducts and loss products use the schema's intermediate role because no byproduct role is available. No end-to-end natural reactor, overall yield or rate constant is claimed.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde cyanohydrin formation

conditions.other: Anoxic water; proposed initial formaldehyde inventory 20-100 mM and total HCN/CN inventory 1-2 equivalents relative to formaldehyde. Maintain pH 6.5-8 and assay over 0.5-24 h rather than assuming quantitative conversion. Use dissolved formaldehyde plus its hydrate as one analytical inventory. Minimize gas exchange and avoid drying untrapped HCN; volatilization competes with capture.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to formaldehyde, followed by proton transfer, producing the C2 cyanohydrin glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Formaldehyde/HCN entry into glycolonitrile-based homologation is supported by Patel et al. (2015) and Xu et al. (2018). The concentrations and residence window here define a proposed operating envelope, not a reported isolated yield. Initial HCN and formaldehyde availability remains an explicit boundary condition; episodic atmospheric production discussed by Wogan et al. (2023) does not establish these aqueous concentrations.

reactions.name: Copper-cyanide and sulfide photoreduction of glycolonitrile to glycolaldehyde
agents: Dissolved copper-cyanide photoredox complexes; transient Cu(I)/Cu(II) cycling, not a mineral-surface catalyst

conditions.other: UV centered near 254 nm; proposed pH 6.5-7.5, glycolonitrile 20-100 mM, total dissolved sulfide 20-200 mM and total dissolved copper 0.1-1 mM. These loadings and a 1-12 h screening window are model test values, not an exact published protocol. Maintain excess cyanide over copper and measure dissolved copper speciation because Cu-sulfide precipitation can remove the photoredox component. Sulfide requires replenishment if volatilization is appreciable. Stop irradiation before carbonyl trapping; settling removes particles but does not remove dissolved cyanocuprates.

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox reduction converts the nitrile group to an imine-level intermediate; hydrolysis releases glycolaldehyde and ammonia. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support sulfide/copper-cyanide photoredox homologation. This edge resolves its nitrile-to-carbonyl chemistry but does not assign a serine-specific yield. S8 is a formal eventual sulfur oxidation inventory; polysulfides and other sulfur species may intervene, and no measured S8 yield is claimed. Catalyst persistence, sulfide delivery and downstream compatibility require experimental verification.

reactions.name: Sulfite-ferrocyanide photoreduction of glycolonitrile to glycolaldehyde
agents: Dissolved hexacyanidoferrate(II), ferrocyanide, as the photoredox component

conditions.other: Anoxic irradiation near 254 nm. The reported network used approximately 100 mM formaldehyde, 200 mM cyanide and 200 mM sulfite, with about 12-12.5 h irradiation. For this separated carbonyl-production stage, proposed pH is 6.5-8, total sulfite/bisulfite 100-200 mM and ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM; the catalyst loading and pH window are test assumptions, not values supplied by the report. Calculate HSO3-/SO3^2- speciation. Sample before extensive secondary homologation and shade the effluent before Strecker conversion or bisulfite storage.

reactions.mechanism: The sulfite-ferrocyanide photoredox system provides reducing equivalents for nitrile reduction; hydrolysis of the reduced nitrogen functionality generates glycolaldehyde and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Xu et al. (2018) demonstrated reductive homologation and quantified downstream products, including serine nitrile. This isolated glycolaldehyde edge is a mechanistic subdivision of that network rather than a separately established preparative yield. Sulfate plus a proton is an atom- and charge-conserving terminal oxidation ledger for bisulfite, not a demonstrated exclusive sulfur-product distribution. Dissolved ferrocyanide availability, iron-cyanide precipitation and UV dose remain important uncertainties.

reactions.name: Thiophosphate photoreduction of glycolonitrile to glycolaldehyde

conditions.temperature: 300-310 K; modeled surface window rather than a reported exact temperature
conditions.other: Reported benchmark: approximately 20 mM glycolonitrile, 20 mM thiophosphate, pH 6.5 and 254-256 nm irradiation for 1 h. Thiophosphate is a consumed reagent, not a catalyst. The unbuffered benchmark is used here; the higher glycolaldehyde yield reported with phosphate buffering is not assumed. Shade after irradiation and transfer promptly to the selected capture step. The listed thiophosphate and phosphate ions represent their acid-base inventories.

reactions.mechanism: Thiophosphate-driven photoreduction of the nitrile functionality, followed by hydrolysis, provides glycolaldehyde and releases reduced nitrogen as ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2023) reported approximately 19% glycolaldehyde and 9% glyceronitrile after 1 h under the cited benchmark, with glycolaldehyde increasing to approximately 34% with phosphate buffering. Phosphate and S8 here are formal eventual oxidation-endpoint bookkeeping, not identified primary photoproducts or measured donor efficiencies. Natural thiophosphate supply and correspondence between mercury-lamp irradiation and sunlight remain unresolved; Ranjan and Sasselov (2017) support surface access to relevant UV wavelengths, not identical reaction rates.

reactions.name: Unprotected glycolaldehyde Strecker conversion

conditions.other: Proposed final pH 9.0-9.3, glycolaldehyde 5-20 mM, total ammonia/ammonium 50-200 mM and cyanide inventory 1-2 equivalents relative to assayed glycolaldehyde. Stop photochemistry before mixing with ammoniacal alkaline seepage. Determine mixing ratios from measured alkalinity; nominal 1:1 mixing would halve organic concentrations and is not assumed to guarantee the required pH. Screen 0.5-24 h and avoid prolonged storage of unprotected glycolaldehyde. The 2 h benchmark in the literature applies specifically to the protected route.

reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde and ammonia form an imine or iminium pool; cyanide addition gives racemic serine aminonitrile, with net water formation.
reactions.reasoning: The aldehyde-ammonia-cyanide Strecker mechanism is supported by Miller (1957), while Ritson et al. (2018) provide serine-specific evidence and demonstrate the advantage of bisulfite protection. Their protected-system conversion time is not treated as a measured rate for this unprotected edge. Carbonyl degradation, ammonia loss and competing cyanohydrin formation can lower selectivity. No mineral catalyst is justified or required.

reactions.name: Reversible bisulfite trapping of glycolaldehyde

conditions.temperature: 300-350 K during a proposed wet-dry storage cycle
conditions.other: Trap near pH 6.5 before evaporation. Proposed bisulfite inventory is 1-2 equivalents relative to measured glycolaldehyde. Begin in water, permit partial drying only after adduct formation, and reconstitute before ammonia addition. The temperature range and 1-24 h cycle are proposed environmental tests; the supplied research does not specify them as its exact protocol. Do not assume trapping protects residual free HCN or removes dissolved photoredox agents.

reactions.mechanism: Bisulfite adds reversibly to the aldehyde carbonyl, forming a covalent hydroxysulfonate reservoir.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson et al. (2018) recovered more than 90% of glycolaldehyde as adduct or hydrate after their pH-6.5 dry-down/reconstitution treatment, whereas unprotected material was largely lost. Bisulfite is therefore represented as a stoichiometric trapping reagent, not a catalyst. Combining this storage chemistry with each upstream photoredox mixture is chemically motivated but has not been demonstrated for every complete sequence represented here.

reactions.name: Formation of the protected glycolaldehyde-ammonia adduct

conditions.other: Reconstitute the bisulfite adduct and adjust to pH 9.2 with ammoniacal alkaline water. Proposed adduct inventory 5-20 mM and total ammonia/ammonium 50-200 mM. The published stability comparison extended to 7 days. Avoid direct UV during storage and measure pH after mixing rather than assuming source-water pH is retained.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible carbonyl release, imine formation and bisulfite addition establish the aminohydroxysulfonate reservoir; the net transformation replaces the carbonyl-derived hydroxyl with an amino group and releases water.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson et al. (2018) showed that the corresponding aminohydroxysulfonate remained stable at pH 9.2 while unprotected glycolaldehyde/ammonia mixtures degraded. The net equation does not claim direct elementary displacement of hydroxide. This intermediate is included because it has experimentally demonstrated storage chemistry, not merely to create another pathway.

reactions.name: Cyanide conversion of the protected adduct to serine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Add cyanide after storage and readjust to pH 9.2. The reported protected mixture converted smoothly within approximately 2 h. Proposed cyanide inventory is 1-2 equivalents relative to measured protected adduct; this ratio is a design assumption. Keep aqueous and shaded. Bisulfite released by conversion remains in solution and can affect subsequent acid demand.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible release of an imine-level intermediate followed by cyanide capture yields serine aminonitrile and regenerates bisulfite.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson et al. (2018) directly demonstrated serine-aminonitrile formation from the stored ammonia/bisulfite system after cyanide addition at pH 9.2. This is among the strongest serine-specific edges in the network. It establishes the aminonitrile endpoint, not free serine or successful downstream mild hydrolysis.

reactions.name: Sulfite-ferrocyanide photochemical imine capture to serine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Use the reported network benchmark of approximately 100 mM formaldehyde-equivalent feed, 200 mM total initial cyanide and 200 mM sulfite, irradiated near 254 nm for about 12-12.5 h. Glycolonitrile is supplied by rxn_001. Proposed pH 6.5-8 and ferrocyanide 0.1-1 mM are test assumptions because those quantitative details are not supplied in the research summary. Do not add an external ammonia reservoir for this branch. Stop irradiation before acidification and account for residual cyanide and sulfur-species acid demand.

reactions.mechanism: Photoreduction produces a glycolaldehyde-imine-level intermediate that can capture additional cyanide before complete hydrolysis, furnishing serine aminonitrile without a separately supplied ammonia reactant.
reactions.reasoning: Xu et al. (2018) reported approximately 4% serine nitrile within a 34% reduced-product fraction. This reaction is a lumped, chemically resolved precursor-forming branch, not a single elementary step; the detailed partition between imine capture and ammonia recycling is not established by that yield. Sulfate and proton outputs are formal terminal redox closure rather than measured exclusive coproducts. The observed 4% must not be interpreted as free-serine yield.

reactions.name: Thiophosphate photochemical formation of serine aminonitrile without added ammonia

conditions.other: Reported benchmark: glycolonitrile and thiophosphate each approximately 20 mM, pH 6.5, HCN present, and approximately 1 h irradiation at 254-256 nm. The supplied summary does not state the HCN concentration; 20-40 mM is a proposed test range, not a reported value. No external NH3 is required in the reaction inputs. Shade and cool immediately after irradiation, then measure residual cyanide before downstream pH changes.

reactions.mechanism: Reductive photochemistry accesses an imine-level C2 intermediate; cyanide capture generates the C3 aminonitrile while retaining HCN-derived nitrogen in the amino-acid precursor.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2023) reported approximately 16% serine nitrile after 1 h when HCN was included, explicitly demonstrating that external ammonia need not supply the amino nitrogen. The edge preserves that distinction from deliberately ammoniacal Strecker chemistry. Phosphate and S8 are provisional eventual oxidation-endpoint bookkeeping, not measured primary photoproducts. Thiophosphate availability, natural photon dose and subsequent environmental hydrolysis remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Hydration of serine aminonitrile to serinamide
agents: Hydrated protons supplied by an acidic volcanic-water reservoir

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2 in a continuously wet, shaded geothermal pool receiving HCl-bearing volcanic condensate. Screen residence times from days to months; no conversion time or yield is established for this exact window. First stop irradiation, allow suspended solids to settle where present, and determine residual cyanide, ammonia and bisulfite inventories. Acidification requires sufficient acid capacity to protonate those inventories; an assumed mixing ratio is not adequate. Any dilution must be propagated into concentrations and rates. This is not a 6 M HCl analytical work-up.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted addition of water to the nitrile, followed by proton transfers, produces the corresponding primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) supports aminonitrile hydrolysis as the origin of accumulated amino acids. Ritson et al. (2018), Xu et al. (2018), and Ritson and Sutherland (2023) establish the upstream serine-nitrile chemistry. Serinamide is a chemically justified hydrolysis intermediate, but the supplied studies do not establish its isolated accumulation or the kinetics of this proposed mild environmental stage. This reaction is an explicit extrapolation and a principal network bottleneck.

reactions.name: Serinamide hydrolysis to free serine
agents: Hydrated protons supplied by an acidic volcanic-water reservoir

conditions.temperature: 353-370 K during proposed hydrolysis; 300-310 K after export
conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2, continuously wet and shaded, with a days-to-months screening window rather than an asserted completion time. Maintain acid capacity as ammonia is released and protonated. After serine becomes detectable, export by cool-water mixing to 300-310 K and approximately pH 5-7; calculate dilution and buffering from measured water compositions. Avoid concentration by prolonged hot drying. A target transfer within hours is an engineering hypothesis, not a demonstrated natural transport timescale.

reactions.mechanism: Water attacks the amide carbonyl; cleavage of the C-N bond gives serine and ammonia, represented in their normalized constitutional forms.
reactions.reasoning: Amide hydrolysis provides the chemically expected free-amino-acid endpoint of the Strecker sequence discussed by Miller (1957). The supplied modern serine-nitrile papers do not demonstrate this complete mild sequence. Rate measurements must show that serine production exceeds precursor loss and product destruction. Andersson and Holm (2000) demonstrate the danger of substantially hotter hydrothermal exposure, supporting cooling and preservation rather than assuming that heating guarantees accumulation.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde Strecker synthesis of glycine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8-9.3, formaldehyde 10-100 mM, total ammonia/ammonium 50-200 mM and total cyanide 1-2 equivalents relative to formaldehyde. Screen 1-48 h without assuming quantitative selectivity. This ammoniacal branch competes with glycolonitrile formation; it is not combined with rxn_001 as though both consume the same carbon inventory independently.

reactions.mechanism: Formaldehyde reacts with ammonia to access methanimine-level species; cyanide addition yields aminoacetonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) establishes aldehyde/HCN Strecker chemistry as a source of amino acids. Kamaluddin et al. (1979) independently observed cyanide, aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide before amino-acid accumulation in a different reaction system. Those observations support the precursor sequence, not the exact proposed concentrations or yields here. No enriched multi-metal seawater mixture is imported because its catalytic necessity was not established.

reactions.name: Hydration of glycine aminonitrile to glycinamide
agents: Hydrated protons from acidic volcanic water

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2, shaded aqueous conditions and days-to-months kinetic screening. Measure residual cyanide and ammonia before mixing with acidic water. Account for acid demand, volatilization and dilution. No rate constant is transferred from high-temperature or strong analytical-hydrolysis experiments.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration yields the primary amide glycinamide.
reactions.reasoning: Kamaluddin et al. (1979) observed aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide as early intermediates, while Miller (1957) supports the general aminonitrile-hydrolysis framework. The proposed low-temperature acidic implementation is an environmental extrapolation, not a reproduced protocol from either study.

reactions.name: Glycinamide hydrolysis to glycine
agents: Hydrated protons from acidic volcanic water

conditions.temperature: 353-370 K for proposed hydrolysis, followed by cooling to 333-353 K
conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2 with days-to-months screening; maintain acid capacity as ammonia is released. Before hydroxymethylation, mix with cooler, less acidic water to reach pH 3.3-3.7 or the separate pH 6-8 operating regime. Formaldehyde is added only after this adjustment. Resulting glycine concentration must be measured rather than inferred from aminonitrile loading.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the amide produces glycine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: The observed glycinamide-before-glycine sequence in Kamaluddin et al. (1979) and the Strecker framework of Miller (1957) support this chemical connection. The exact environmental residence time and yield remain unverified. Separating hydrolysis from formaldehyde addition prevents an unsupported assumption that all stages share one compatible pH.

reactions.name: Glycine C-alpha hydroxymethylation to serine

conditions.temperature: 333-353 K at pH 3.3-3.7; alternatively 323 K at pH 8 or 343 K at pH 6
conditions.other: The listed temperature/pH pairs are supported experimental regimes, not a continuous interchangeable range. Proposed screening inventories are glycine 10-100 mM and formaldehyde 1-10 equivalents, with 1-14 day sampling; those loadings and times are not supplied as exact source protocols. Use a shaded aqueous pool, not dry heating. Cool and dilute after product formation, and quantify glyoxylate, methylated products and remaining glycine alongside serine.

reactions.mechanism: A multistep carbonyl/amine network permits C-alpha carbon-carbon bond formation between glycine and formaldehyde, giving net hydroxymethylation. A single established elementary mechanism is not asserted.
reactions.reasoning: Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) observed serine from glycine/formaldehyde in weakly acidic water at 60-80 degrees C without an inorganic solid phase. Mohammed et al. (2017) characterized related chemistry at 50 degrees C/pH 8 and 70 degrees C/pH 6, including competing transamination and N-methylation. This is an experimentally supported non-Strecker serine-forming step, but it is not selective or guaranteed to dominate the mixture.

reactions.name: Proposed photochemical HCN entry to glycine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed total HCN/CN 20-100 mM, total sulfide 20-200 mM, dissolved copper 0.1-1 mM, pH 6.5-7.5 and UV near 254 nm. Screen 0.5-12 h and quantify aminoacetonitrile directly before hydrolysis. These values define a mechanistic test, not a reported glycine-aminonitrile protocol. Monitor copper-sulfide precipitation, sulfide loss and competing imine hydrolysis to formaldehyde.

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of HCN to a methanimine-level intermediate, followed by capture of another cyanide unit, can furnish aminoacetonitrile. Sulfide supplies the required reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: Explicitly a mechanistic extrapolation: Patel et al. (2015) support HCN photoredox homologation and amino-acid-precursor chemistry, but the supplied research does not establish this separately operated aminoacetonitrile branch or its yield under the stated conditions. It is included as the lower-confidence alternative nitrogen/carbon entry for P10, not as a tenth independently verified serine mechanism. S8 is only formal terminal redox bookkeeping.

reactions.name: Competing glycine-formaldehyde transamination

conditions.temperature: 323 K at pH 8 or 343 K at pH 6
conditions.other: Competes with rxn_016 in the mildly warm glycine/formaldehyde mixture. Use the same measured initial inventories and time series when estimating branching; do not assign both reactions complete conversion of the same glycine. No branching fraction is specified.

reactions.mechanism: Condensation, proton transfer and imine hydrolysis transfer the amino functionality from the glycine-derived carbon skeleton to the formaldehyde-derived carbon, formally producing glyoxylate and methylamine.
reactions.reasoning: Mohammed et al. (2017) experimentally support nonenzymatic transamination of glycine with formaldehyde and glyoxylate formation. Methylamine is the chemically balanced amino-acceptor coproduct in this net representation; the supplied summary does not provide its yield or a complete product balance. This explicit competing branch prevents treating glycine hydroxymethylation as selective.

reactions.name: Optional hydrothermal serine-loss initiation by dehydration
agents: Pyrite-pyrrhotite-magnetite assemblage as experimental redox context, not an established serine-dehydration catalyst
K-feldspar-muscovite-quartz assemblage as experimental proton-activity buffer

conditions.other: Optional nonproductive exposure, excluded from all ten target-producing sequences. The temperature, pressure and mineral-buffer context follow the reported stability experiments. Hot proton activity was mineral-buffered; the supplied report gives no numerical pH or rate constant. A proposed 0.1-24 h sampling series would test loss kinetics but is not a published lifetime. No hydrogenation edge or unsubstantiated hydrogen-activation catalyst is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Formal elimination of water gives dehydroalanine as a proposed transient intermediate in serine destruction; its isolated accumulation is not assumed.
reactions.reasoning: Andersson and Holm (2000) measured serine destruction and formation of glycine and alanine under hydrothermal conditions, consistent with a dehydration/reduction interpretation. This individual dehydration edge is explicitly an inferred mechanistic loss term, not direct proof that dehydroalanine accumulated. It documents the preservation hazard without forcing any productive pathway through a hot vent or asserting an unsupported mineral-catalyzed hydrogenation mechanism.

pathways.name: Copper-sulfide carbonyl production followed by immediate Strecker conversion
pathways.description: Formaldehyde and HCN furnish glycolonitrile. Copper/sulfide photoreduction supplies glycolaldehyde, which is promptly combined with ammonia and cyanide without a storage stage. Serine formation then requires the explicitly proposed amide-resolved hydrolysis and cooling sequence. The complete staged sequence is not experimentally demonstrated.

pathways.name: Copper-sulfide carbonyl production with bisulfite storage
pathways.description: The same photochemical carbonyl source is followed by covalent bisulfite storage and formation of the experimentally supported ammonia-bisulfite adduct before cyanide addition. This is a storage-dependent alternative to P1, not an independent carbon-skeleton mechanism. Compatibility of residual copper/sulfur species with the storage sequence remains to be tested.

pathways.name: Sulfite-ferrocyanide carbonyl production followed by immediate Strecker conversion
pathways.description: Glycolonitrile enters sulfite-ferrocyanide photoreduction. Glycolaldehyde is captured in a separately adjusted ammoniacal Strecker stage rather than relying on in situ photochemical aminonitrile formation. Photon dose, carbonyl survival, mixing dilution and subsequent hydrolysis control the achievable flux.

pathways.name: Sulfite-ferrocyanide carbonyl production with bisulfite storage
pathways.description: Photogenerated glycolaldehyde is trapped before concentration or delayed use. Sulfite/bisulfite has distinct roles as upstream reductant and downstream reversible carbonyl-trapping reagent; sufficient residual or replenished inventory must be measured. Protected Strecker conversion is followed by the conditional environmental hydrolysis endpoint.

pathways.name: Thiophosphate carbonyl production followed by immediate Strecker conversion
pathways.description: The experimentally supported thiophosphate/glycolonitrile photochemical carbonyl stage is followed by immediate ammonia/cyanide addition after pH adjustment. The glycolaldehyde benchmark supports precursor formation, not a measured yield for this full sequence to free serine.

pathways.name: Thiophosphate carbonyl production with bisulfite storage
pathways.description: Thiophosphate photochemistry supplies glycolaldehyde, while separately supplied bisulfite provides a chemically distinct storage function. Reconstitution, ammonia addition and cyanide capture precede hydrolysis. The combined thiophosphate-product/bisulfite-storage mixture has not been validated end to end.

pathways.name: Sulfite-ferrocyanide in situ serine-aminonitrile branch
pathways.description: Glycolonitrile and additional cyanide enter the photochemical branch associated with approximately 4% observed serine nitrile. Unlike P3 and P4, this route does not require a separately operated glycolaldehyde/ammonia stage. Subsequent hydrolysis is represented explicitly and is not included in the reported nitrile yield.

pathways.name: Thiophosphate in situ serine-aminonitrile branch without added ammonia
pathways.description: Glycolonitrile, HCN and thiophosphate feed the experimentally observed approximately 16% serine-nitrile branch. The nitrogen source does not require external ammonia. Free serine remains conditional on the subsequent amide-resolved hydrolysis and preservation stages.

pathways.name: Classical glycine precursor synthesis followed by hydroxymethylation
pathways.description: Formaldehyde, ammonia and HCN first build glycine aminonitrile. Hydrolysis through glycinamide supplies glycine, which receives a further formaldehyde-derived carbon to produce serine. This uses the experimentally supported non-Strecker serine-forming step, but upstream mild hydrolysis and competing glycine transamination limit the complete route.

pathways.name: Proposed photochemical glycine-precursor entry followed by hydroxymethylation
pathways.description: HCN photoreduction and cyanide capture are proposed to provide glycine aminonitrile without an externally supplied ammonia reactant at that entry step. Hydrolysis supplies glycine, and separately available formaldehyde supplies the third serine carbon. The rxn_017 entry is explicitly less well supported than the other precursor-forming branches and requires direct validation before this pathway can be treated as experimentally established.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon-skeleton construction is chemically credible. Patel et al. (2015) supports copper-cyanide/sulfide photoredox homologation, and glycolaldehyde Strecker chemistry is well established. Immediate capture could limit glycolaldehyde degradation, but its timing and compatibility with the photochemical mixture are unspecified. The principal target-achievement gap is an operationally demonstrated rxn_011/rxn_012 sequence that produces and preserves free serine under surface-compatible conditions. The formal S8 output is balanced bookkeeping, not an experimentally established coproduct distribution.
suggestions: Specify substrate concentrations, copper-cyanide loading and speciation, pH, temperature, irradiation spectrum and photon exposure.
Measure glycolaldehyde capture versus degradation in the actual photochemical mixture.
Demonstrate aminonitrile hydration and serinamide hydrolysis under a stated environmental history, directly measuring free serine and competing losses.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The storage branch addresses a demonstrated chemical problem rather than merely adding connectivity. Ritson et al. (2018) supports glycolaldehyde bisulfite protection, the ammonia adduct, and cyanide conversion to serine aminonitrile. However, integrating that chemistry with copper/sulfide photochemical effluent is not demonstrated here. Published storage and Strecker conditions must be distinguished from an assigned operating protocol. Protection improves precursor persistence but does not resolve the shared serinamide-to-free-serine bottleneck.
suggestions: Specify storage duration, water activity, pH adjustment and cyanide addition using the demonstrated bisulfite chemistry as an experimental reference.
Test protection and cyanide conversion with residual copper, sulfide and photochemical coproducts present.
Validate downstream hydrolysis and serine survival rather than extrapolating storage or aminonitrile yields to free-serine yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Xu et al. (2018) supports sulfite/ferrocyanide reductive homologation, although the reported chemistry produces a mixture rather than establishing selective delivery of glycolaldehyde into this complete sequence. The subsequent Strecker step is plausible. Ferrocyanide availability, irradiation conditions, pH and carbonyl-capture kinetics are not assigned in the reaction records. Sulfate formation is an explicitly provisional terminal redox representation. Free-serine production remains conditional on rxn_011 and especially rxn_012.
suggestions: Specify ferrocyanide loading, sulfite speciation, substrate concentrations, photon exposure and pH control.
Quantify the glycolaldehyde available for Strecker capture rather than assigning the entire photochemical product fraction to this branch.
Establish hydrolysis conditions and residence times that yield free serine without excessive precursor or product destruction.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This combines experimentally supported photoredox and protected-Strecker modules from Xu et al. (2018) and Ritson et al. (2018). Their connection is chemically reasonable, but an uninterrupted implementation is not supplied. Sulfite consumed as reductant must be distinguished quantitatively from bisulfite retained for reversible carbonyl storage. That is an inventory and kinetic requirement, not a conservation violation. The protected sequence supports serine-aminonitrile formation more strongly than it supports subsequent accumulation of free serine.
suggestions: Track sulfur allocated to photoreduction, residual trapping reagent and terminal oxidation products.
Specify a physically justified pH and storage history, and test protected Strecker conversion in the photochemical product matrix.
Measure serinamide formation, its hydrolysis rate and final free-serine recovery under the selected surface conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ritson and Sutherland (2023) directly supports glycolaldehyde production from glycolonitrile and thiophosphate, with approximately 19% glycolaldehyde reported without the yield-enhancing phosphate-buffer condition and approximately 34% with buffering. Those observations support rxn_004, not an integrated free-serine yield. Subsequent ammonia/cyanide capture is credible but needs testing in this mixture. The phosphate/S8 outputs are appropriately qualified as formal bookkeeping. Hydrolysis and preservation remain the decisive unresolved endpoint requirements.
suggestions: Choose and specify a buffered or unbuffered implementation; declare any required initial buffer inventory rather than assuming product phosphate supplies it.
Test immediate Strecker capture with residual thiophosphate and its photoproducts.
Validate conversion through serinamide to directly measured free serine under explicit pH, temperature and residence-time conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Thiophosphate carbonyl production and bisulfite-protected Strecker chemistry each have strong experimental support in Ritson and Sutherland (2023) and Ritson et al. (2018), respectively. Connecting them is a reasonable proposal, not an independently demonstrated complete route. The bisulfite branch offers evidence-based precursor protection, but its behavior in a thiophosphate-derived mixture and the required pH history remain unspecified. All productive transformations can plausibly occur in surface settings; the broad environment label alone does not establish their operating compatibility.
suggestions: Demonstrate bisulfite trapping and protected Strecker conversion using an actual thiophosphate photochemical mixture.
Specify storage, pH adjustment and reagent activities, including acid-base speciation.
Show that subsequent hydrolysis produces recoverable free serine and does not simply redistribute material among nitrile, amide and degradation products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Xu et al. (2018) directly reported approximately 4% serine aminonitrile within a broader sulfite/ferrocyanide photochemical product mixture. This supports the central precursor-forming branch and does not require inventing an unbalanced ammonia source. Nevertheless, rxn_009 is a lumped photochemical transformation rather than a fully resolved elementary mechanism. Neither that precursor yield nor the balanced equation demonstrates free-serine production. The downstream hydrolysis sequence and natural irradiation/concentration regime remain insufficiently specified.
suggestions: Annotate rxn_009 as an experimentally supported net branch with the reported substrate mixture, irradiation conditions and product distribution.
Quantify serine-aminonitrile recovery and competing reactions in the retained photochemical matrix.
Demonstrate surface-compatible nitrile and amide hydrolysis, distinguishing directly present serine from serine released during analytical work-up.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-supported target-precursor branch: Ritson and Sutherland (2023) reported approximately 16% serine aminonitrile after one hour with HCN present in thiophosphate photochemistry. Its nitrogen accounting is sound without externally added ammonia. The experimental result provides unusually direct support for rxn_010, but remains a nitrile result rather than a free-serine result. The selection of this pathway as best rests on that substrate-specific evidence, not its step count or reagent identity. Hydrolysis and preservation still prevent high-confidence end-to-end approval.
suggestions: Assign explicit operating conditions, distinguishing the published millimolar, pH-6.5, 254-256-nm experiment from any proposed natural photon exposure and concentrations.
Characterize sulfur/phosphorus coproducts before using the formal phosphate/S8 outputs in quantitative redox or kinetic models.
Demonstrate serinamide formation and hydrolysis with a measured free-serine mass balance and simultaneous loss measurements.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Classical glycine Strecker synthesis and hydrolysis provide a credible precursor route. Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) and Mohammed et al. (2017) support serine formation from glycine and formaldehyde, so rxn_016 is more than a formal carbon-balance proposal. Importantly, this pathway does not depend on the serinamide bottleneck shared by P1-P8. Its limitations are unassigned glycine-precursor hydrolysis conditions and the selectivity of hydroxymethylation. The explicit rxn_018 transamination competitor is appropriate, but additional formaldehyde-driven side chemistry remains relevant.
